title: What Happens During a Final Walkthrough Before Closing in California
content_html:
What the Final Walkthrough Is For

The final walkthrough is the buyer's last chance to see a home before taking ownership of it. It typically happens within a day or two of closing, after the seller has moved out (or is in the final stages of moving) and after any repairs negotiated earlier in the transaction are supposed to be complete. It is not a second home inspection. Its purpose is narrower: confirming that the property is in the condition the purchase agreement promised, not uncovering new problems from scratch.

For buyers coming out of the escrow process, the walkthrough can feel like a formality squeezed between loan approval and signing. It isn't. It's one of the few remaining points where a buyer can flag an issue before money changes hands and the deal becomes much harder to unwind.

When the Walkthrough Happens

Most purchase agreements specify a window — often a day or two before the scheduled closing date — during which the buyer or the buyer's agent can walk through the property one final time. Scheduling it too early risks missing last-minute moving damage; scheduling it too close to closing leaves little time to address anything found. Your agent typically coordinates the timing directly with the listing agent once a closing date is set.

What Buyers Should Check

A thorough final walkthrough generally covers the following areas:

  • Agreed-upon repairs: If the seller agreed to fix anything as a result of the home inspection or subsequent negotiations, verify the work was actually done — ideally with receipts or invoices, not just a visual check.
  • Systems and appliances: Run the HVAC system, test faucets and toilets, open and close doors and windows, and turn on any appliances included in the sale. Confirm they work the way they did when the offer was made.
  • Included items: Check that any fixtures, appliances, or personal property the seller agreed to leave behind — per the purchase agreement — are still present. Sellers sometimes remove items by mistake, or occasionally on purpose.
  • General condition and cleanliness: Look for new damage that wasn't there during the inspection — scuffed walls or flooring from the move, damaged landscaping, or anything that suggests the home wasn't maintained between inspection and closing.
  • Move-out completion: Confirm the seller's personal belongings and trash have been removed, or are on track to be removed by the agreed date, per the purchase agreement's possession terms.
  • Utilities on: Ask that utilities remain on through the walkthrough so systems can actually be tested — a dark, powered-down house makes it hard to verify much of anything.

What It Is Not

It's worth repeating: the final walkthrough is not an opportunity to renegotiate the deal or raise objections to conditions that were already known and disclosed during the inspection period. If a buyer accepted a property's condition, or didn't request a repair for something found during inspection, the walkthrough isn't the moment to revisit that decision. It's meant to confirm continuity of condition — that nothing has changed for the worse since the buyer last agreed to move forward — not to reopen negotiations on issues the buyer already had a chance to address through contingencies in the purchase agreement.

If Something Is Wrong

If the walkthrough turns up a genuine problem — a promised repair wasn't done, an included appliance is missing, or there's new damage — the buyer's agent should raise it immediately with the listing agent, before closing proceeds. Depending on the issue and the stage of the transaction, options generally include:

  • Delaying closing until the issue is resolved
  • Negotiating a credit at closing to cover the cost of fixing it
  • Arranging for funds to be held in escrow until the repair is completed
  • In rare, serious cases, reconsidering whether to proceed with the purchase at all

What a buyer should generally avoid is closing anyway and simply hoping the seller follows up afterward. Once a sale closes and the deed records, the buyer's leverage to get something fixed largely disappears. Any outstanding issue is far easier to resolve in the hours before closing than in the weeks after.

Why It Matters Even When Everything Looks Fine

In most transactions, the final walkthrough is uneventful — sellers move out cleanly, repairs get done, and nothing has changed. That's exactly why it's easy to treat as optional. But the cost of skipping it, or rushing through it, is asymmetric: it takes relatively little time in the vast majority of cases, and the rare time something is wrong, catching it before closing can save a buyer real money and hassle compared to catching it after.

Preparing for the Walkthrough

Buyers get the most out of a final walkthrough by bringing a copy of the purchase agreement, the inspection report, and any repair agreements or invoices the seller provided. Comparing the home against these documents, item by item, is more reliable than relying on memory of what the house looked like weeks earlier. A buyer's agent who was present for the inspection can also help spot anything that looks different.
